full_judgment:
2. The petitioner's case arises out of an ostensible non-payment of dividend and his inability to partake of the profits in respect of and in proportion to 500 shares owned in the Company. It is also alleged that the Company has not paid to the petitioner "the share from other income" of the Company. It is shown that the petitioner's ownership of 506 shares in the Company has come to be judicially recognised in Other Suit No. 276 of 1990 and as upheld in Other Appeal No. 387 of 1993. The judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court in Other Appeal No. 387 of 1993 came to be challenged in Civil Revision No. 2709 of 1994 in which this Court in its judgment dated 29-4-2002 discharging the Rule upheld the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court made in confirmation of the judgment and decree in Other Suit No. 296 of 1990 (Annexure-'B'). This led the petitioner to address a legal notice dated 10-2-2003 demanding his share of profit with 15% interest amounting to Taka 18,32,18,750 calculated for a period of 41 years i.e., from 1962-2002 (Annexure-'C'), A response dated 4-3-2003 was addressed to the petitioner wherein some of the respondents, including the respondent No.2, generally disputed the petitioner's claimed entitlement (Annexure-'C'). It is stated variously in the Application that either the respondent Nos. 2 and 4 jointly or the respondent No.2 individually from his personal resources paid Taka 36,00,000 to the petitioner, ostensibly by way of partial payment of the total claim of the petitioner as to dividend and share of profits and earnings of the Company, such payment being made from April, 2004 to November, 2005. The petitioner has produced a copy of a bank statement showing receipt of such payments into his bank account (Annexure-'B-1'). The schedule of claim as found in the Application shows that the adjusted claim of the petitioner upon receipt of the above-referred payment stands at Taka 17,96,18,750. It is alleged that the Company having thereafter failed and neglected to make payment of what it terms as "its admitted debt" the petitioner thereafter sent another legal notice dated 28-5-2005. under section 242 or the Act by registered post to the Company and the other respondents seeking a payment of the claimed balance amount of Taka 17,96,18,750 (Annexure-D' and 'D-1 '). 

 7. The learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr M Rezaul Hasan has submitted at the outset that the Company having failed to make payment on the petitioner's claim within the period of three weeks further to the notice dated 25-5-2005 (Annexure- 'D'), and the condition of section 242(1)(i) of the Act having been satisfied in that regard, it is clear that thereby the precondition for filing this Application under section 241(v) has been fulfilled. In this regard, Mr Hasan submits that the payment of Taka 36,00,000 has indeed, been made, but only against the dividend entitlement of the petitioner as well as against the profit earnings of the Company and not by way of a consideration contemplated under the agreement dated 26-6-2004 (Annexure-'X') Mr Hasan disputing the authenticity of this agreement and of it being in evidence of an alleged transfer of the petitioner's entire share holding in the Company. Even though Mr Hasan has at length argued on the lack of authenticity of the said agreement and the Forms-117 with a view to impressing upon this Court that the petitioner remains to this date the owner of 500 shares in the Company, the main thrust of his argument has been as to the continued entitlement of the petitioner to the dividend and share in profits and earnings of the Company against the backdrop of the Company operating to this date as a solvent, viable entity. In that regard, he submits, and thereby adopts a position contrary to the reservation expressed in this Application as to the capacity of the Company to pay its admitted debt, that the case of the petitioner is, that the Company continues to be an entity in operation earning profit but which has failed nevertheless to make payments of dividend to the petitioner and for permit him to partake of his share in the profits of the Company such a situation having been brought about specifically by the machinations of the Board of Directors acting primarily to secure their own interest and for their personal gain much to the intended prejudice of the petitioner's legitimate interests. This fact, coupled with that of the respondents having collectively resorted to alleged acts of fraud and forgery to project the petitioner as having already divested himself of all interests in the Company pursuant to the agreement dated 26-6-2004 (Annexure-'X') has led the learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr Hasan to submit further that the Court must deduce from these facts and circumstances that the Company is being managed in a manner by the respondents that would justify a judicial finding on such respondents directors being guilty of misconduct and abuse of powers with a view to securing their own interests and depriving the petitioner from his legitimate share of the income of the Company. In this regard, Mr Hasan submits that it would additionally be for this Court to arrive at a finding that it would be just and equitable for an order of winding up to be made under section 241 (vi) of the Act. In this retard, Mr Hasan has referred to the judgment in Daulat Makanmal Luthria vs Solitaire Hotels reported in 1993 Company Cases, Vol. 76, 215 in support of the view that this Court's discretion to so wind up a company under section 241(vi) is largely dependent on its opinion of the merits of each given case. The criterion for such an exercise of this Court's discretion, Mr Hasan submits, is well explained in the following observations made in the Daulat Makanmal Luthria Case at page 229: 

 8. Given the criterion so pointed out by Mr Hasan as above and the provisions of section 2A1 of the Act, it has become necessary for this Court at the outset to determine the parameters of the exercise of both its jurisdiction and discretion to wind up the Company in the given facts and circumstances. Primacy in this regard has been accorded by this Court to a consideration of the competing views and arguments made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner and that of the respondents as to whether circumstances exist in this case to order a winding up of the Company. In this regard, this Court is readily reminded of the caution expressed by KM Hasan, J in Mohiul Islam vs Century Properties Dey reported in 7 BLC 248 of "killing of a Company" prematurely. That cautionary note so expressed by this Court manifests the existence of certain common law safeguards that have been devised in this regard to protect companies from premature and unwarranted demise in the face of what may be termed as "unreasonable" demands made in the form of prayers for winding up (Jose J. Kadavil vs Malabar Industrial Co Ltd reported in 1986 Company Cases, Vol. 59, 969). In this regard, this Court has taken note of the generally accepted principle, and as endorsed in cases like Ripon Press and Sligar Mill Co Limited, vs V Gopal Chetti reported in AIR 1932 (PC) 1 and Motiur Rahman vs May Industries Ltd. reported in 37 DLR 41, that nonpayment of dividend is per se not recognised as a proper ground for winding up of a company. The next step is to see whether such non-payment of dividend when and where ostensibly attributable to mismanagement and internal irregularities and omissions in the administration of the Company by its directors would necessarily strengthen the cause of winding up. It is noted that even in such instances this Court has been reluctant in the past to interfere in the manner of granting a winding up order. The view that has gained currency in this regard has perhaps, been best encapsulated by the judgment in Rehana Ahmed vs Nahar Shipping Lines Ltd reported in 44 DLR 256 where the ratio of this Court's judgment as encapsulated in the head note of the case report reads thus : 

 "There may be certain irregularities and omissions in the management of a company. But mere allegation of mismanagement will not make the company liable to be wound up on the just and equitable reason. Where nothing more is established than that the directors have misappropriated the funds of the company an order for winding up would not be just and equitable. Allegations of misconduct of the directors or that the business has been carried on at a heavy loss are per se not grounds on which the Court would order winding up. Where petition by a share-holder contains allegations which all relate to the internal management mismanagement of the company's affairs, it is a matter for the share-holders themselves to deal with and not one that would call for interference by the Court." 

 9. The dicta about having excluded various scenarios as otherwise relied upon by the petitioner to justify in the facts and circumstances of this case the making of a winding up order, the learned Advocate for the respondents Mr Ashanul Karim, submits that the fundamental test of winding up involves one of examining whether a Company is insolvent or not. That test came to be elaborated thus in Agrani Bank vs Bangladesh Tyres Ltd reported in 43 DLR (AD) 164 where in his judgment ATM Afzal J applied thus the concept of a missing substratum coupled with the notice of insolvency as the fundamental basis for an order of winding up: 

 A winding up order is called for under section 162 Clause (vi) of the Act if the Court is of the opinion that it is just and equitable that the Company should be wound up. Such opinion is bound to gain ground when it is found that the substratum of the Company was gone or its only business had become impossible. The substratum of a company will be deemed to be gone when (a) the subject matter of the Company is gone or (b) the object for which it was incorporated has substantially failed or (c) it is impossible to carry on the business of the Company except at a loss, that is, there is no reasonable hope of trading at a profit. The facts of the instant case show that here is a Company which has ceased functioning for years together, has been in very heavy debts to various creditors and, as far as the present appellant in concerned, has not taken any step ever since the statutory notice and thereafter over the years for repayment of the debts which has gone on mounting. Truly, the substratum of the Company is gone." 

 Applying the test above, and given the tenor of the submission made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, it is this Court's view that the petitioner in this case has been unable to show that the Company has on any material date been Insolvent. Rather, on the contrary, the basic premise of the petitioner's case is that the Company is a going concern having earnings from which profit has accrued and to which the petitioner must be found to have a due entitlement and share in. If that scenario is to be accepted, and there being nothing in the petitioner's case to show to the contrary in this regard, then it becomes incumbent upon the petitioner to show further and as laid down by Mainur Reza Chowdhury, J in Mazharul Haque vs Bulk Management reported in 48 DLR 453 "that he would derive any advantage or minimise some disadvantage" should the winding up prayed for materialise. It was further held in the Mazharul Haque Case, and following the dictum in Re Chesterfield Catering Co Ltd reported in (1976) All ER at page 294, than any lapse or failure to so substantiate the justification for winding up, will necessarily call into question the very locus standi of the petitioner to petition as he  has done for winding up the Company. Applying that test to these facts and circumstances, it is Unclear to this Court how the winding up of the respondent No. 1 Company shall prove to be advantageous or beneficial to someone as the petitioner who is basically laying a claim to shares in the earning and profits of a profit-making entity. Concomitantly, in these circumstances, it becomes redundant for the petitioner to show that the winding up of the Company would minimise any risk exposure that he may have as a member contributor. Indeed, and as evident from the Application and the Affidavit-in-Reply, the petitioner has not made out his case in either regard, In fact, the case as made out by the petitioner alludes to the fact that the continued existence of the Company as a viable entity would instead inure to the benefit of the petitioner. 

 Upon a reading of the Schedule of Claim, in particular, in this Application reproducing the contents of the notices of claim served upon the Company, and without anything in this case to show otherwise and that such claim and the breakdown of its components are objectively assessable and have indeed, been so evaluated and assessed, this Court is left with a distinct impression that the claim reads as but a tally of random figures and dates appealing purely to and being a product of the petitioner's subjective perception, of his case. It is in that light that this Court is satisfied of the fact that this Application is a misconceived one and that it would have served the petitioner to consider seeking other more appropriate remedies, if at all available, properly and duly. In this regard, it has also not been lost on this Court that the crux of the petitioner's case is that his entitlement to a share in the income and profits of a going concern has been thwarted by the respondents, directors deliberately operating to his detriment and in a maimer that amounts to misconduct. This Court, as above referred, has clearly held in the Rehana Ahmed Case that such ground cannot qualify as a proper ground for winding up under section 241 of the Act. In such circumstances, a long list of cases show that a proper remedy may instead lie in seeking relief against oppression resulting from misconduct and mismanagement or relief pursued more appropriately in a civil Court rather than readily opting for an extreme remedy of winding up (S Kumar Bansal vs UP Mineral Products Ltd reported in 1996 Company Cases Vol. 87 223). Instead, and as submitted by Mr Karim, that insistence, however, on the part of the petitioner to a winding up of the Company even given the above circumstances may lead this Court to deduce that the petitioner is acting unreasonably in seeking to have the Company wound up instead of pursuing other possible remedies (See, Jose J Kadavil vs Malabar Industrial Co. Ltd reported in 1986 Company Cases, Vol. 59, 969). This Court is thus of the opinion that should the petitioner have .been able to show that the winding up of the Company is the only remedy under the circumstances or that indeed, he has no other remedy available to him, then it would have been possible for him to rely on section 241 (vi) to have the Company wound up on just and equitable grounds, but that too, however, only as a last resort and at the discretion of this Court. Clearly, the petitioner has failed to satisfy this Court in that regard. In this regard, this Court notes that the test of winding up on just and equitable grounds is one, and as sufficiently laid down in Hind Overseas Pvt. Ltd vs RP Jhunjhunwalla reported in AIR 1Q76 (SC), 565, of a balance struck between the interests of shareholders as a whole as well as that of the Company and in which equation the interest of the petitioner alone may not be accorded a primacy of consideration. In this regard, the Indian Supreme Court held thus in the Hind Overseas Pvt. Ltd Case at paragraph 34 at 574. 

 This Court notes that the concern as to protecting the goodwill of a Company as well as the interests of all other shareholders in general has concomitantly also led to the development of substantial jurisprudence endorsing the view that event admission of winding up applications are to be granted sparingly and not as a matter of rule. Accordingly in, In re Atul Drug House Ltd Case reported in 1971 Company Cases, Vol. 41 352 the Gujarat High Court accordingly held: 

 It is this Court's finding that there is nothing in the petitioner's case that has satisfied this Court of the overriding need, in the facts and circumstances, to allow the petitioner's interests to be given such primacy of consideration. On the contrary, it appears that allowing this Application will amount to the petitioner's sole interests running roughshod over that of the Company and the other shareholders without proper justification.
